Reproducing Hadjas et al. (2025) from dandiset 001528¶

Paper. Hadjas LC, Kollman GJ, Linderhof L, Xia M, Mansur S, Saint-Pierre M, Lim B, Lee EB, Cicchetti F, Awatramani R, Hollon NG, Hnasko TS (2025). Parkinson's Disease-vulnerable and -resilient dopamine neurons display opposite responses to excitatory input. bioRxiv, doi:10.1101/2025.06.03.657460. This attempt used the full text of the preprint (version 1, CC BY), which has no data or code availability statement.

Dandiset. DANDI:001528, version draft. The dandiset has no published version, and the paper cites none, so the draft is the only version there is. The draft read here was last modified on 2026-09-01T15:27:47Z (290 assets); the first cell below checks the draft's modification time against that and prints whether it has changed. A draft can change, so the numbers below hold for that state of it.

What the dandiset holds. Fiber photometry with optogenetic stimulation of STN or PPN inputs to the substantia nigra in 120 mice: SNr GABA neurons, SNc pan-DA neurons, GRAB-DA in DLS and TS, DA terminals in DLS and TS, Vglut2+ DA neurons and Anxa1+ DA neurons (Figures 2 to 5, S3, S4). Each file holds the lab's dF/F, the 465 and 405 nm signals and the stimulation epochs. The human tissue counts of Figure 1 and Figure S1 are not in it.

Code read. The dandiset links its conversion code, catalystneuro/hnasko-lab-to-nwb at commit deaefa7b1776a5ffb98fd50c5ff4d7b899bdaf59 (the lotfi_2025 conversion, its metadata, and a Python re-implementation of the lab's MATLAB pipeline with a description of the MATLAB scripts), and an example notebook in dandi/example-notebooks at commit 77a123e54e0d185e37768603da1faff79b62421f (001528/HnaskoLab/Lotfi_2025), which shows how to load the files. The lab's MATLAB scripts are not public.

Outside inputs. None. Groups, inputs and sites come from the files' own metadata.

No random numbers are drawn anywhere in this notebook.

The files hold 120 mice, each in one group, which fits the dandiset's summary (120 subjects). The group of each file is read from its experiment description, the site from the name of its dF/F series, and the input from the name of its opsin (ChrimsonR in STN or PPN). For the Anxa1 mice, nine have separate DLS and SNc files (session ids ending in _DLS and _SNc), and nine have one pair of files without a site suffix, whose dF/F series and raw signal are named SNc; the fiber photometry table of every Anxa1 file lists both an SNc and a DLS fiber. Every session start time has the offset -00:01, the local mean time of London that pytz gives when a time zone is attached with replace; the true offset is lost (a metadata error, it does not affect the analysis). Eight subject ids are written in lower case (c3015 and others) while the others are upper case.

    dt = np.diff(r["dff_t"])
    rows.append({"path": r["path"], "protocol": r["protocol"], "dff_unit": r["dff_unit"], "gc_unit": r["gc_unit"],
                 "n": len(r["dff"]), "t0": r["dff_t"][0], "dt_median_ms": 1000 * np.median(dt),
                 "regular": bool(np.all(np.abs(dt - 0.01) < 1e-6) or (np.abs(dt[dt < 1] - 0.01) < 1e-6).all()),
                 "longest_gap_s": dt.max(), "same_times": np.array_equal(r["dff_t"], r["gc_t"]) and np.array_equal(r["dff_t"], r["af_t"]),
                 "timestamps": r["dff_has_timestamps"], "nan_frac": np.isnan(r["dff"]).mean(),
                 "dff_p01": np.nanpercentile(r["dff"], 0.1), "dff_p999": np.nanpercentile(r["dff"], 99.9),

All 100 Hz series start at 0 s and are sampled every 10 ms; the dF/F and the two signals share one time base. Some files of the frequencies protocol join separate recordings: their timestamps jump (up to about two days, below) and the joins are filled with missing values. The dF/F is stated in "a.u.", and the series description gives (Gc - fitted_af) / fitted_af; its values (for example 99.9th percentiles of 1.7 to 249) are in percent, as in the MATLAB pipeline (dF = 100 * (Gc - fit) / fit), and the recomputation below confirms this. The unit is a metadata error; the analysis uses the values as percent.

The epoch tables give 5 mW at 635 nm for every train, as the Methods state, and the number of pulses in each train fits its frequency and length. The intervals between trains are 10 s in the durations sessions and 20 s in the frequencies sessions (offset to next onset), as the Methods state; the files' session description of the frequencies protocol says 10 s, which the data do not support. Three things differ from the Methods. First, 13 mice (SNr GABA and SNc pan-DA mice with ids starting with B) have 10 trials per condition, where the Methods state 5. Second, 30 mice (SNr GABA, pan-DA and DA terminal mice recorded on the rig with a 24 kHz raw rate) also have 16 s trains, which the paper does not mention; they are not used. Third, 14 frequencies sessions have no 4 s trains (the 13 mice above, and C4608, whose 4 s block the conversion notes describe as a separate recording that is not in the dandiset). Fifteen epochs are dropped: nine zero-length entries and six trains whose window runs past the end of the recording or across a gap. The conversion code (convert_session.py) names the 1 s block of the STN to SNr GABA frequencies sessions s1s10mW, which suggests 10 mW, while the epoch tables and the Methods give 5 mW; the data cannot settle this.

# Recordings deposited twice: identical dF/F, or near-identical traces of the same length.
md5 = pd.Series({r["path"]: r["dff_md5"] for r in recs})
print("Files sharing an identical dF/F array:", int(md5.duplicated(keep=False).sum()))
by_len = {}
for r in recs:
    by_len.setdefault(len(r["dff"]), []).append(r)
pairs = []
for n, rs in by_len.items():
    for i in range(len(rs)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(rs)):
            a, b = rs[i]["dff"], rs[j]["dff"]
            ok = np.isfinite(a) & np.isfinite(b)
            if ok.sum() > 100 and np.corrcoef(a[ok], b[ok])[0, 1] > 0.99:
                pairs.append((rs[i]["path"], rs[j]["path"]))
print("Pairs of same-length files with dF/F correlation above 0.99:", pairs)
starts = info.groupby(["subject", "session_start"]).size()
print("Mice with two files starting at the same time:", starts[starts > 1].index.tolist())

The stored dF/F agrees with a recomputation from the stored 465 and 405 nm signals following the Methods (biexponential fit of the 405 nm signal, scaled to the 465 nm signal by robust regression, in percent): median correlation 0.9999 in durations sessions and 0.9988 in frequencies sessions, above 0.99 in 217 of 258 files, with a median absolute difference below 0.1 % dF/F. This is consistent with the stored series being the lab's dF/F in percent. In a few files the two differ more (correlation down to 0.31), where the fit of a segment differs; the lab's exact fitting options are not public. The analysis uses the stored dF/F.

# Clock check: responses at the true onsets against onsets shifted by -3 s and +3 s (within the
# 10 to 20 s between trains). Per recording, the mean over conditions of |during - pre|.
def abs_response(r, shift):
    ct = ph.condition_traces(r, shift=shift)
    vals = [abs(ph.window_mean(c.trace, c.t, 0, c.duration) - ph.window_mean(c.trace, c.t, -c.duration, 0))
            for _, c in ct.iterrows()]
    return float(np.mean(vals)) if vals else np.nan

clock = pd.DataFrame([{"path": r["path"], "subject": r["subject"], "group": r["group"], "input": r["input"], "site": r["site"], "protocol": r["protocol"],
                       **{f"shift_{s:+.0f}": abs_response(r, s) for s in (0.0, -3.0, 3.0)}} for r in recs])
clock["ratio"] = clock["shift_+0"] / clock[["shift_-3", "shift_+3"]].max(axis=1)
print("Median |during - pre| (% dF/F) at true and shifted onsets, and the median ratio true / largest shifted:")
print(clock.groupby(["group", "protocol"])[["shift_+0", "shift_-3", "shift_+3", "ratio"]].median().round(2).to_string())
print("\nRecordings whose true-onset response exceeds both shifted ones:", int((clock.ratio > 1).sum()), "of", len(clock))
print("Recordings where it does not (the clock could not be shown from the response):")
print(clock[clock.ratio <= 1][["path", "group", "input", "site", "shift_+0", "shift_-3", "shift_+3"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
print("\nRecordings where it does not, by group, input and protocol:")
print(clock[clock.ratio <= 1].groupby(["group", "input", "protocol"]).size().to_string())

In every group the median response at the true onsets is larger than at onsets shifted by 3 s either way (median ratio 1.2 to 6.3 by group and protocol), and in 235 of 258 recordings the response at the true onsets exceeds both shifted ones. The epoch tables share the clock of the dF/F. The 23 recordings listed last, mostly SNc pan-DA recordings with small and variable responses and unsuffixed Anxa1 recordings, are those where the clock could not be shown from the response; they are used as they are. By input, they include three PPN pan-DA durations recordings (C3164, C5007, C5008), four STN pan-DA durations recordings, two DA terminal DLS recordings and one frequencies recording each of GRAB-DA DLS and Vglut2 STN.

The paper reports Anxa1+ DLS terminals in 8 (STN) and 10 (PPN) mice and SNc cell bodies in 5 and 4. The dandiset holds DLS recordings for 5 and 4 mice, the mice that also have an SNc file, and SNc-labeled recordings for 8 and 10. The paper's DLS counts equal the dandiset's mice with a DLS file plus those with an unsuffixed file (5 + 3 and 4 + 6), and its SNc counts equal the mice with both files. Two explanations fit the counts: the unsuffixed recordings are DLS recordings labelled SNc, or the dandiset lacks the DLS recordings of nine mice and holds SNc recordings the paper did not analyse ("cell body signals were only detected in a subset of mice"). The signals favour the second: the unsuffixed recordings resemble the SNc recordings of the dual mice (small inhibition, no rebound, similar variability), not their DLS recordings (larger inhibition and a rebound). The tests of figs4-anxa1-soma-inhibited and fig5-anxa1-dls-inhibited below bear on this too: the paper's cell-body statistics are matched by the dual mice's SNc recordings alone, and its terminal statistics are not matched by adding the unsuffixed recordings to DLS. This is consistent with, but does not prove, that the labels are right and that the DLS recordings of nine mice are missing. The analysis keeps the dandiset's labels and shows the other reading as a variant.

The response measures, per mouse and condition, are computed once here and used by every claim.

For 1 s trains the pre-stimulus window (1 s before onset) is the baseline window, so pre is 0 by construction (printed above). Every paired test of a 1 s train against its pre-stimulus window is therefore a one-sample test of the response against 0, and in the two-way mixed ANOVAs on 1 s trains the site F equals the site by time interaction F. The paper's two-way ANOVA values show the same pattern (site F 40.9 and interaction of the same size).

In [10]:
def cohort(group, inp, site=None, protocol="durations", duration=1.0, frequency=40.0, kind=None):
    """One row per mouse: the response measures for one condition."""
    q = (R.group == group) & (R.input == inp) & (R.protocol == protocol) & np.isclose(R.duration, duration) & np.isclose(R.frequency, frequency)
    if site is not None:
        q &= R.site == site
    if kind is not None:
        q &= R.kind == kind
    out = R[q]
    assert not out.subject.duplicated().any(), "a mouse appears twice"
    return out.set_index("subject")

def freq_matrix(group, inp, duration, site=None, kind=None, measure="during"):
    """Mice x frequency (5, 10, 20, 40 Hz) matrix of one measure, frequencies protocol."""
    q = (R.group == group) & (R.input == inp) & (R.protocol == "frequencies") & np.isclose(R.duration, duration)
    if site is not None:
        q &= R.site == site
    if kind is not None:
        q &= R.kind == kind
    m = R[q].pivot_table(index="subject", columns="frequency", values=measure)
    return m.reindex(columns=list(ph.FREQUENCIES))

def fmt(res):
    keep = {k: (round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in res.items()}
    return ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in keep.items())

def plot_traces(ax, group, inp, site=None, protocol="durations", duration=1.0, frequency=40.0, kind=None, label=None):
    q = (R.group == group) & (R.input == inp) & (R.protocol == protocol) & np.isclose(R.duration, duration) & np.isclose(R.frequency, frequency)
    if site is not None:
        q &= R.site == site
    if kind is not None:
        q &= R.kind == kind
    paths = R[q].path.tolist()
    traces = []
    for r in recs:
        if r["path"] in paths:
            ct = ph.condition_traces(r)
            c = ct[np.isclose(ct.duration, duration) & np.isclose(ct.frequency, frequency)].iloc[0]
            traces.append(c.trace)
            t = c.t
    m = np.vstack(traces)
    mean, sem = np.nanmean(m, axis=0), np.nanstd(m, axis=0) / np.sqrt(len(m))
    ax.plot(t, mean, label=f"{label or site} (n={len(m)})")
    ax.fill_between(t, mean - sem, mean + sem, alpha=0.3)
    ax.axvspan(0, duration, color="red", alpha=0.08)
    ax.set_xlim(-3, 8)
    return float(np.nanmin(mean)), float(np.nanmax(mean))

Result: not reproduced. 10 of 16 counts match. The SNr GABA, pan-DA and GRAB-DA groups match exactly, as do DA terminals in TS (9) and Vglut2 PPN (10). DA terminals in DLS have 8 mice (paper 9) and Vglut2 STN 9 (paper 10). The four Anxa1 counts differ: DLS 5 and 4 against 8 and 10, SNc 8 and 10 against 5 and 4. All four Anxa1 counts would match if the unsuffixed recordings were DLS recordings; the data check and the Anxa1 claims below favour the reading that the paper's DLS recordings of those nine mice are not in the dandiset. For Vglut2 STN the paper's own Wilcoxon statistics fit 9 mice: W = 41, 43 and -5 give exact p = 0.0117, 0.0078 and 0.82 with n = 9 (the paper's 0.012, 0.008 and 0.82) and 0.037, 0.027 and 0.85 with n = 10, so the legend's 10 is likely an error in the paper, not a missing mouse. Counted that way 11 of 16 match, still below 12. The DA terminal mice recorded in TS (9) and DLS (8) are different mice, so the data do not show which DLS mouse is absent.

Result: reproduced. For 1 s trains the response rises from 5 to 40 Hz for STN (4.07 to 32.66 %, Friedman 21.00, p = 0.00011, 40 Hz above 5 Hz in 7 of 7 mice) and PPN (1.57 to 6.10 %, 18.15, p = 0.00041, 8 of 8), the paper's values to the first decimal. The repeated-measures ANOVA variant gives p = 0.014 and 0.0001, and 0.25 s trains give the same Friedman values.

fig3b-da-stn-250ms-peak¶

A 250 ms 40 Hz train of STN inputs elicits a net increase in SNc pan-DA neuron activity that peaks after stimulus offset (latency to peak 0.50 +/- 0.03 s, mean +/- SEM).

print(f"Net response over 0 to 1.25 s: mean {net.mean():.2f} % (range {net.min():.2f} to {net.max():.2f}), t {res.statistic:.2f}, p {res.pvalue:.2g}")
print(f"Variant, peak window 0 to 1.25 s: mean latency {short.mean():.3f} s, SEM {short.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(short)):.3f}")

Result: partially reproduced. With the fixed window (peak from onset to 2.25 s) the mean latency is 0.786 s (SEM 0.204, n = 11), outside 0.50 +/- 0.03 s, because two mice peak at the window's end (C4217 at 2.03 s and B8612 at 2.24 s). Ten of 11 mice peak after offset and the net response over 0 to 1.25 s is positive (2.89 %, t = 3.28, p = 0.0083). With a window ending 1.25 s after onset (a variant, which does not change the outcome) the mean latency is 0.492 s, SEM 0.033, the paper's value. The two late-peaking mice have small responses (ranges -1.44 to 2.02 % and -0.92 to 1.15 % from -1 to 5 s), an early local maximum at 0.41 and 0.62 s (1.28 and 0.30 %), and a slow rise that keeps going past the window (maximum over 0 to 5 s at 2.97 and 2.78 s). This looks like a late rebound or slow drift, not the early peak, and C4217 is one of the recordings whose clock could not be shown in the data check.

fig3c-da-stn-duration¶

For SNc pan-DA neurons the STN-evoked response varies with train duration; with 1 and 4 s trains an initial increase is followed by inhibition (Friedman test, F = 13.0, p = 0.005).

def duration_tests(group, inp, site):
    rows = {}
    for d in [0.25, 1.0, 4.0]:
        c = cohort(group, inp, site, duration=d)
        rows[d] = c
    during = pd.DataFrame({d: rows[d].during for d in rows})
    auc = pd.DataFrame({d: rows[d].auc for d in rows})
    print("Mean during (%) per duration:", during.mean().round(2).to_dict(), "| mice:", len(during))
    out = {}
    out["a"] = ph.friedman(during.values)
    out["b"] = ph.friedman(np.column_stack([rows[1.0].pre.reindex(during.index).values, during.values]))
    out["c"] = ph.friedman(auc.values)
    for k, v in out.items():
        print(f"   reading ({k}): Friedman chi2 {v['stat']:.2f}, df {3 if k == 'b' else 2}, p {v['p']:.2g}, n {v['n']}")
    return rows, out

rows, out = duration_tests("panDA", "STN", "SNc")

for r in recs:
    if r["path"] in rows[4.0].path.values:
        ct = ph.condition_traces(r); cc = ct[np.isclose(ct.duration, 4.0) & np.isclose(ct.frequency, 40.0)].iloc[0]
        early.append(ph.window_mean(cc.trace, cc.t, 0.0, 0.5)); late.append(ph.window_mean(cc.trace, cc.t, 3.0, 4.0))
early, late = np.array(early), np.array(late)
res = stats.ttest_rel(early, late)
print(f"4 s trains: mean over 0 to 0.5 s {early.mean():.2f} %, over 3 to 4 s {late.mean():.2f} %; paired t {res.statistic:.2f}, p {res.pvalue:.2g}, n {len(early)}")
print(f"Mice with late below early: {int((late < early).sum())} of {len(early)}; with late below 0: {int((late < 0).sum())}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
for d in [0.25, 1.0, 4.0]:

ax.set_xlabel("s from onset"); ax.set_ylabel("dF/F (%)"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

def site_contrast(group, inp, duration=1.0):
    ts, dls = cohort(group, inp, "TS", duration=duration), cohort(group, inp, "DLS", duration=duration)
    res = ph.mixed_2x2(ts.pre, ts.during, dls.pre, dls.during)
    print(f"{group} {inp} {duration} s: TS n {len(ts)} mean during {ts.during.mean():.2f} % (mice above 0: {int((ts.during > 0).sum())}); "
          f"DLS n {len(dls)} mean during {dls.during.mean():.2f} % (mice below 0: {int((dls.during < 0).sum())})")
    print(f"   site F{res['df']} {res['F_site']:.1f}, p {res['p_site']:.2g}; interaction F {res['F_interaction']:.1f}, p {res['p_interaction']:.2g}")
    return ts, dls, res

def frequency_tests(group, site, plan, direction, kind=None):
    """plan: list of (input, duration, test name, paper text). direction +1: 40 Hz above 5 Hz."""
    out = []
    for inp, dur, test, paper in plan:
        m = freq_matrix(group, inp, dur, site, kind=kind)
        res = ph.friedman(m.values) if test == "Friedman" else ph.rm_anova(m.values)
        other = ph.rm_anova(m.values) if test == "Friedman" else ph.friedman(m.values)
        diff = np.nanmean(m[40.0] - m[5.0])
        ok = res["p"] < 0.05 and np.sign(diff) == direction
        incomplete = m[~np.isfinite(m.values).all(axis=1)]
        dropped = "; ".join(f"{s} lacks {'/'.join(f'{f:g}' for f in row.index[row.isna()])} Hz" for s, row in incomplete.iterrows())
        out.append({"input": inp, "duration": dur, "test": test, "mice": len(m), "n": res["n"], "stat": round(res["stat"], 2),
                    "p": res["p"], "mean_5": m[5.0].mean(), "mean_10": m[10.0].mean(), "mean_20": m[20.0].mean(),
                    "mean_40": m[40.0].mean(), "holds": ok, "paper": paper, "other_test_p": other["p"], "max_friedman": 3 * res["n"], "dropped": dropped or "-"})
    t = pd.DataFrame(out)
    print(t.round(4).to_string(index=False))
    print("Tests that hold:", int(t.holds.sum()), "of", len(t))
    return t

plan = [("STN", 0.25, "RM", "F2,8 = 7.5, p = 0.02"), ("STN", 1.0, "RM", "F2,7 = 13.6, p = 0.004"), ("STN", 4.0, "RM", "F2,9 = 16.9, p = 0.001"),
        ("PPN", 0.25, "Friedman", "F = 20.0, p = 0.0002"), ("PPN", 1.0, "Friedman", "F = 24.0, p < 0.0001"), ("PPN", 4.0, "Friedman", "F = 23.2, p < 0.0001")]
ts_freq = frequency_tests("GRABDA", "TS", plan, +1)

In TS all six tests find an effect of frequency with the 40 Hz mean above the 5 Hz mean: STN repeated-measures ANOVA F = 7.62, 13.76 and 17.31 (p = 0.019, 0.0044, 0.0011; paper 7.5, 13.6, 16.9) and PPN Friedman 19.80, 24.33 and 23.27 (p = 0.0002 or below; paper 20.0, 24.0, 23.2).

The paper gives F1,11 = 12.8 for both STN and PPN 1 s trains, with p = 0.0005 and 0.002; F(1, 11) = 12.8 gives p = 0.0043

Result: reproduced. In DLS all six tests find an effect of frequency with the 40 Hz mean below the 5 Hz mean (p from below 0.0001 to 0.013). STN 0.25 s and 4 s give F = 7.89 and 47.23 (paper 7.5 and 46.8), PPN 0.25 s Friedman 11.53 (paper 12.3) and PPN 1 s F = 12.98 (paper 12.8). STN 1 s gives F = 26.17, where the paper reports F1,11 = 12.8 with p = 0.0005, the same F and df as it reports for PPN 1 s with p = 0.002; F(1, 11) = 12.8 gives p = 0.0043, so one of the two entries in the paper is likely a copy.

Result: not reproduced. For 1 s trains at 5 Hz (Figure 4E and 4H, the reading fixed in the criterion) the mean GRAB-DA signal in DLS during the train is positive but not significantly so for either input: STN 1.51 % (4 of 7 mice above 0, p = 0.22), PPN 1.40 % (6 of 9, p = 0.13). The sentence also cites Figure S3F and S3L, the 4 s DLS frequency panels. In 4 s trains at 5 Hz the signal is above 0 for STN (5.41 %, 7 of 7, p = 0.00062) and not significantly for PPN (2.01 %, 6 of 9, p = 0.07), 1 of 2 inputs, which would be partially reproduced under that reading; it does not change the outcome. The 0.25 s trains (Figure S3E and S3K, not cited) show no increase (p = 0.49 and 0.76). The 1 s after offset is positive in every condition (0.96 to 6.76 %), as the paper's account of summed rebounds would predict.

fig5-vglut2-excited¶

Stimulation of STN or PPN inputs increases the activity of Vglut2+ DA neurons in SNc (STN, Wilcoxon, 0.25 s W = 41, p = 0.012, 1 s W = 43, p = 0.008, 4 s W = -5, p = 0.82; PPN, paired t-test, 0.25 s t = 2.9, p = 0.02, 1 s t = 3.4, p = 0.008, 4 s t = 3.0, p = 0.01).

In [25]:
def pre_during_tests(group, site, plan, kind=None, label=""):
    out = []
    for inp, dur, test, paper in plan:
        c = cohort(group, inp, site, duration=dur, kind=kind)
        res = ph.wilcoxon_w(c.during, c.pre) if test == "Wilcoxon" else ph.paired_t(c.during, c.pre)
        other = ph.paired_t(c.during, c.pre) if test == "Wilcoxon" else ph.wilcoxon_w(c.during, c.pre)
        out.append({"input": inp, "duration": dur, "test": res["test"], "n": res["n"], "stat": round(res["stat"], 2), "p": res["p"],
                    "mean_during": c.during.mean(), "mean_pre": c.pre.mean(), "mice_up": int((c.during > c.pre).sum()),
                    "mean_post": c.post.mean(), "paper": paper, "other_test_p": other["p"]})
    t = pd.DataFrame(out)
    print(label); print(t.round(4).to_string(index=False))
    return t

plan = [("STN", 0.25, "Wilcoxon", "W = 41, p = 0.012"), ("STN", 1.0, "Wilcoxon", "W = 43, p = 0.008"), ("STN", 4.0, "Wilcoxon", "W = -5, p = 0.82"),
        ("PPN", 0.25, "t", "t = 2.9, p = 0.02"), ("PPN", 1.0, "t", "t = 3.4, p = 0.008"), ("PPN", 4.0, "t", "t = 3.0, p = 0.01")]
vg = pre_during_tests("Vglut2", "SNc", plan)
core = vg[vg.duration < 4]

for ax, inp in zip(axes, ["STN", "PPN"]):

Result: reproduced. The four tests the claim rests on find an effect of frequency with the 40 Hz mean above the 5 Hz mean: STN 0.25 s (Friedman 13.53, p = 0.0036) and PPN 0.25, 1 and 4 s (11.23, 17.91 and 16.20; p = 0.011, 0.0005 and 0.0010). The PPN tests use 7 of 10 mice: C3412, C3798 and C4707 have no 5 Hz trains in the dandiset. The Friedman statistic over four conditions is at most 3n, and the paper's 24.8 for PPN 1 s needs at least 9 mice, so the paper had 5 Hz trains for mice whose 5 Hz trains are not deposited. As in the paper, STN 1 s and 4 s are not significant (p = 0.43 and 0.16; paper 0.11 and 0.07).

Paper t = 6.4, p = 0.0004: two-sided p with df {3: np.float64(0.0077), 4: np.float64(0.0031), 7: np.float64(0.0004), 9: np.float64(0.0001)}
Paper t = 3.9, p = 0.004: two-sided p with df {3: np.float64(0.0299), 4: np.float64(0.0175), 7: np.float64(0.0059), 9: np.float64(0.0036)}
Paper t = 3.8, p = 0.004: two-sided p with df {3: np.float64(0.032), 4: np.float64(0.0191), 7: np.float64(0.0067), 9: np.float64(0.0042)}

Result: blocked (data missing). Anxa1 DLS terminals fall during the train: no STN mouse (of 5) goes up in any condition, and no PPN mouse (of 4) except one in 4 s trains. But the dandiset holds DLS recordings for 5 (STN) and 4 (PPN) mice, where the paper has 8 and 10. At these numbers the Wilcoxon tests the paper uses for three of the six conditions cannot reach p < 0.05 (smallest attainable p 0.0625 for 5 mice and 0.125 for 4), so "reproduced" (6 of 6) cannot be reached with the deposited mice. The three t-tests can reach it, so "partially reproduced" (3 to 5 of 6) could be reached; 2 of 6 tests are significant, the two t-tests other than PPN 4 s (p = 0.13). The paper's statistics fix its n: W = -36 and -55 are -n(n+1)/2 for n = 8 and 10 (every mouse down; exact p 0.0078 and 0.0020), and t = 6.4 with p = 0.0004 needs 7 df (8 mice), where 4 df give p = 0.0031. With the unsuffixed recordings added to DLS (a variant), all 6 tests are significant. Its STN 4 s Wilcoxon gives the paper's W = -36, but the other two W (-34 and -51 against -36 and -55) and the three t values (2.65, 2.47 and 2.98 against 6.4, 3.9 and 3.8) are not the paper's, so those recordings are not the paper's DLS data. The DLS recordings of nine of the paper's mice are not in the dandiset, and the outcome is blocked for that reason.

Result: partially reproduced. Two of the paper's Friedman entries do not fit their p-values (F = 11.5 gives p = 0.0093 against the stated 0.0002; F = 15.5 gives 0.0014 against 0.015), and the Figure 5 legend says the STN panels (N, O) show no significant effect of frequency while the Results report one for all three STN durations.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. It uses the lab's dF/F stored in the files, the Methods' 1 s baseline, and windows the Methods do not give: the mean during the train, a pre-stimulus window of the train's length, and the 1 s after offset. Where a panel shows one train duration without saying which, the 1 s train is used. The paper chose between parametric and non-parametric tests by a Shapiro-Wilk test; here each comparison uses the test the paper reports for it. Repeated-measures ANOVAs are Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, as the paper's fractional degrees of freedom imply. For many comparisons this reproduces the paper's statistic to the first decimal, which suggests the windows match the lab's. The Anxa1 groups follow the dandiset's site labels.

For 1 s trains the pre-stimulus window is the baseline window, so tests of a 1 s train against its pre-stimulus window are tests against 0.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • It holds the photometry of Figures 2 to 5, S3 and S4 for 120 mice; the human tissue counts of Figure 1 and S1 and the histology of Figure S2 are not in it.
  • For the Anxa1 mice it holds DLS terminal recordings for 5 (STN) and 4 (PPN) mice where the paper has 8 and 10, and SNc recordings for 8 and 10 where the paper has 5 and 4. The nine extra SNc recordings carry no site suffix in their file names; their signals resemble the SNc recordings, and the paper's cell-body statistics are matched by the other SNc recordings alone. The DLS recordings of nine mice appear to be missing.
  • DA terminals in DLS have 8 mice (paper 9). Vglut2+ neurons with STN stimulation have 9 mice where the legend gives 10, but the paper's Wilcoxon statistics fit 9, so the legend is likely wrong.
  • Three Vglut2 PPN mice (C3412, C3798, C4707) have no 5 Hz trains, while the paper's Friedman statistic needs at least 9 mice with all four frequencies.
  • The dF/F is stated in "a.u." but is in percent.
  • Thirteen mice have 10 trials per condition (Methods: 5), 30 mice have 16 s trains the paper does not mention, and 14 frequencies sessions have no 4 s trains, one of them (C4608) because a separate recording was not converted.
  • Every session start time carries the offset -00:01, an artefact of attaching the London time zone with replace, so the true offset is lost; eight subject ids are lower case.
  • The files' description of the frequencies protocol gives an interval of 10 s between trains; the epochs and the Methods give 20 s.
  • The conversion code names the 1 s block of the STN to SNr GABA frequencies sessions as 10 mW, while the files and the Methods give 5 mW.
  • The epoch tables share the clock of the dF/F (the responses lock to the true onsets in 235 of 258 recordings), and no recording is deposited twice.
  • The dandiset has no published version, so results hold for the draft as modified on 2026-09-01.
